claims.statement: On 2026-10-07 the attribution-to-block chain ran end to end for the first time, but the approval phrase was typed by Claude under an explicit authorisation given in conversation rather than on stdin, so r7 recorded that limitation verbatim. On 2026-10-08 13:56Z the same chain was run again with Jesse typing the phrase himself: all nine checks passed, rc=0, chain_demonstrated=True, the kernel set carried 192.168.0.141, the counter moved and revocation left an empty set confirmed by querying the kernel. Claude did not touch that process; it only cleared stuck processes beforehand, re-opened the ICMP traffic source, and watched the kernel nft table count go 1 to 0 from the out-of-band management link before reading the artifacts. The finding that matters is not that the rerun passed but that the two runs are indistinguishable from their outputs: both artifacts carry the identical authorization block, authority_came_from='human approval phrase on stdin' and human_phrase_supplied=true. The program cannot tell who pressed the key, which is exactly why provenance has to be carried outside the artifact rather than asserted by it.

claims.statement: Enforce stack readiness had been failing three times out of three at 236-247 seconds, and the supervisor logged it as 'the enforce stack will not come up'. The root cause was 94 orphaned `ros2 run demo_nodes_cpp talker` processes left behind by the campaign's own unauthorized_participant runner, roughly 31 per session. A prediction was written before clearing them: if the talkers are the cause, readiness should pass afterwards. After `wsl --shutdown` the same `live_stack.sh start enforce` reported READY in 87 seconds with zero residual nodes, and the following 80 complete sessions were 80/80 eligible with zero SIGKILL and zero hard-stop. The mechanism by which they escaped is the one C2C-082 wrote down in advance as the fork-teardown risk: the parent exits unconditionally, so ManagedProcess.stop sends SIGTERM to a process group whose leader has already gone. C2C-082 predicted this would degrade to 'nothing gets reaped, no worse than before'; measurement showed it is worse than before, because the cost accumulates - median in-session wall clock went 126s to 337s over 3.5 hours until the pace breaker stopped the campaign by itself, and that breaker's judgment checked out (85.7 + 0.376 x 158.8 = 145.4s predicted against 337.0s measured, residual +192 against a threshold of 90, with throughput falling 28.5 to 23.2 sessions per hour as an independent corroboration). The fix is that the supervisor's backstop sweep listed sixteen process patterns and every one of them was a defender process, so it could never count an attacker-side orphan; a seventeenth pattern was added, and the test that prevents recurrence derives the expected pattern set from runners.py rather than hard-coding it.
claims.title: Enforce readiness failed because of 94 talker orphans the campaign created itself

claims.statement: The runbook written on 2026-10-03 had never been executed. Running it on 2026-10-15 produced the project's first identification numbers on a sealed, never-opened holdout: feature extraction over 3,553 sessions in 1:57:28 with ru_maxrss 1.50 GiB and zero swaps; per-mode splitting giving permissive 1,606 and enforce 1,947 sessions, bit-identical to the campaign's own count arrived at by a completely different path; four seals created, two for `split == test` and two for `novelty_role`, whose scopes turned out to be orthogonal rather than nested (intersection 22 and 23 sessions) so that 'open once' needed no relaxation and no resolution was lost; identification balanced accuracy 0.4655 for permissive over 18 classes with a ceiling of 1.0000 and zero zero-recall classes, and 0.4228 for enforce over 20 classes; open-set session recall at k=2 of 0.1645 for permissive with a normal false-unknown session rate of exactly 0.0; and the deployment gates evaluated with minimum_1100_independent_sessions True for the first time in both modes, item-for-item matching the prediction recorded on 10-02 that finishing the campaign would turn exactly one of the eleven gates. independent_final_test is True for the first time in this project, and deployment_eligible remains false in both modes. Two structural findings came out of the run itself. The runbook omitted an entire phase: features.py writes only a single fused table, while the `split` and `novelty_role` columns that the seals bind are produced by per_mode_split.py, so sealing was impossible without it. And the enforce open-set evaluation was refused with rc=4 because its scorer is undecided, with the seal still unopened and no artifact written, because check_settings is ordered before require_unopened - which is the first live evidence for the one-shot protection the runbook claims.
claims.title: The four-phase retrain runbook ran end to end, and it was missing an entire phase

limitations: Everything here is permissive. Enforce's CV, 1-NN and batch effect were not measured.
'Stack instance' is a time-window proxy: nothing records an instance id. The two-hour saturation matches the batch scale, but the supervisor log was not read to pair sessions to stack_up events.
The three-hour window has 67 sessions, about 4.5 per class, so its 1-NN of 0.7164 is not comparable to refresh 640's 0.9490 at 17 per class; what is comparable is the scale-free ratio.
The microscopic mechanism is not identified: what varies in the 'benign background' - Gazebo initial conditions, machine load, code_revision, SHM residue - was not measured. Only its scale was.
Standardisation uses whole-table mean and standard deviation; that choice affects absolute values, though the ratio and 1-NN are less sensitive to it.
Nothing here produces a new acceptance number, and the holdout figures the two percentage downgrades rest on did not change.
claims.statement: The gap between the session-level cross-validation score of 1.0000 and the sealed holdout's 0.4655 was first framed as a failure to transfer from CV to holdout. That framing put two different datasets on one line. Measuring session-level CV on dataset_mega itself, with --eval-split train_validation and the tool reporting test_rows_used 0, gives 0.5124 against a shuffled control of 0.0523 and a chance level of 0.0556. So the CV-to-holdout step transfers well, a difference of -0.047 that sits inside the resolution, and the drop of -0.49 is between the datasets. The cause is the data geometry, not the learner: leave-one-out 1-NN, which involves no fitted model at all, gives 0.9490 on refresh 640 against 0.4670 on mega, while random forest gives 1.0000 against 0.5124, so the forest beats nearest neighbour by only 0.045, and the two agree on which classes are worst. Four candidates were ruled out. The program: the same tool reproduces 1.0000 plus/minus 0.0000 on refresh 640 with a worst class of 1.000. Any single feature: zeroing sros_auth_fail_rate, which is non-zero in 97.4 percent of refresh rows and identically zero across all 38,810 mega rows, and then also mean_bytes_per_packet, still leaves refresh at 1.0000. The class count: restricting mega to the same fifteen classes moves the between-to-within ratio from 0.588 to 0.591. The sample size: the direction is wrong, since going from 17 to 65 sessions per class should bring the nearest neighbour closer. The session jitter added on 09-20 was also ruled out, and from inside mega so that nothing else varies: Spearman correlations between within-class standardised distance and jitter magnitude are all about zero, with warmup at -0.070, and splitting on quartiles leaves the high-jitter group with the smaller within-class radius. What is left is measured rather than inferred. Same-class pair distance saturates within about two hours and is then flat across eighteen days, which is a step and not a drift, and two hours is one batch at forty sessions of ninety to a hundred and thirty seconds with one stack_up per batch. Restricting mega to a single three-hour window gives a within-class radius of 6.176, a between-centroid distance of 13.442 and a ratio of 2.177, against refresh 640's 6.478, 13.871 and 2.141 - nearly bit-for-bit - and the ratio falls monotonically with window length from 1.492 at three hours to 0.588 over the whole span. So the earlier 1.0000 measures how separable attacks are against one stack instance's benign background, and 0.4655 is the realistic number. The direction this implies is background-invariant features or per-deployment calibration, not more data and not a better learner.
claims.title: The earlier 1.0000 was a single-batch ceiling, not a generalisation result
